Stem borers are among the most economically damaging pests in Philippine rice agriculture. The adult moths lay egg masses on rice leaves, and upon hatching, the larvae bore directly into the stem. In young plants, this kills the central shoot, a condition called “deadheart,” where the leaf turns yellow and can be easily pulled out. In mature plants, larval feeding at the stem base severs the connection to developing grains, producing bleached, empty panicles called “whitehead.” Several species attack rice, including the striped stem borer (Chilo suppressalis) and the yellow stem borer (Scirpophaga incertulas). Infestations are worst during the early vegetative and late booting stages. Losses can reach 30–50% of yield if left unmanaged.

• Egg Mass: Females lay flat, scale-like egg masses of 50–150 eggs on the upper surface of rice leaves, usually near the midrib; eggs hatch in 5–7 days. 

• Larva (inside stem): Newly hatched larvae immediately bore into the stem and feed internally; they pass through 5–6 instars over 20–30 days, causing deadheart in young plants or whitehead in mature ones. 

• Pupa (inside stem): Pupation occurs inside the dead stem or tiller; this resting stage lasts 7–10 days. 

• Adult Moth: Adults emerge, live for only 5–7 days, and mate immediately; females begin laying egg masses within days. 

• Total cycle: 30–40 days.
• Conserving and releasing parasitic wasps (e.g., Trichogramma) that destroy pest eggs.\n\n• Protecting natural predators like spiders and ground beetles.

• Synchronous planting across the community to break the pest cycle.

• Harvesting crops at ground level to remove overwintering pupae.

• Plowing and flooding fields immediately after harvest.
• Applying systemic insecticides (e.g., Cartap hydrochloride) only if "deadheart" damage exceeds the 10% economic threshold during the vegetative stage.

Armyworms (Mythimna separata and related species) are highly destructive caterpillars in the family Noctuidae that are notorious for mass-feeding events. Their name comes from their behavior of moving in large groups across fields like marching armies when food is scarce. Newly hatched larvae feed on the margins of leaves, but older instars (especially the 5th and 6th) consume entire leaves and even the panicle. A single larva can destroy several tillers in its lifetime. They tend to feed at night and hide in the soil during the day, making detection difficult. Outbreaks are common after prolonged dry spells followed by rain, and in the Philippines they pose a serious threat during the wet season. Severe infestations can strip entire paddies in a matter of days.

• Egg: Females lay eggs in clusters of 100–300 on leaf surfaces; eggs hatch in 4–6 days. 

• Larva (6 instars): Early instars feed on leaf margins; later instars (5th and 6th) consume entire leaves and panicles—feeding at night and hiding in the soil during the day; larval stage lasts 14–21 days. 

• Pupa (soil): Larvae burrow into the soil to pupate; the pupal stage lasts 8–10 days. 

• Adult Moth: Adults emerge, feed on nectar, and reproduce rapidly. 

• Total cycle: ~30 days.
• Utilizing naturally occurring Nucleopolyhedrovirus (NPV) which specifically infects armyworm larvae.\n\n• Encouraging predatory birds and natural wasps.

• Flooding seedbeds to drown caterpillars.

• Deep plowing fields after harvest to expose soil-dwelling pupae to the sun.

• Digging trenches around uninfected fields to prevent marching larvae from entering.
• Spraying foliar insecticides (like synthetic pyrethroids) preferably in the late afternoon when larvae actively feed, but only during severe outbreaks.

Planthoppers, particularly the Brown Planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens), are one of the most serious insect pests of rice in Asia. Both nymphs and adults feed by inserting their needle-like mouthparts into the phloem tissue at the base of the stem to extract sap. Heavy feeding causes “hopperburn,” a condition where infested areas of the field suddenly turn orange and dry up. Beyond direct damage, planthoppers also serve as vectors for Grassy Stunt and Ragged Stunt viruses, which can devastate entire crops. They reproduce rapidly under warm, humid, and nitrogen-rich canopy conditions, and certain biotypes have developed resistance to commonly used insecticides. In the Philippines, they are a leading cause of widespread crop losses, often triggered by the resurgence of populations after broad-spectrum pesticide use eliminates their natural predators.

• Egg (leaf sheath): Females insert rows of eggs into the tissue of the leaf sheath, close to the waterline; eggs hatch in 7–10 days. 

• Nymph (5 instars): Nymphs are active from the moment they hatch and begin feeding on phloem sap immediately; each instar lasts 2–4 days for a total of 15–20 days; early instars are wingless, later instars develop wing pads. 

• Adult: Adults may be long-winged (macropterous, capable of migration) or short-winged (brachypterous, flightless); they continue feeding and reproducing. 

• Total cycle: 20–30 days.
• Strictly conserving spiders, mirid bugs, and aquatic beetles which are highly effective natural hunters of hoppers.

• Planting resistant rice varieties.

• Implementing Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) to deny them a continuous humid environment at the stem base.

• Avoiding excessive nitrogen fertilizer which causes dense, humid canopies.
• Using selective insecticides (e.g., Buprofezin). Crucial warning: Avoid broad-spectrum chemicals that kill spiders, as this directly causes hopper resurgence.

Leafhoppers, especially the Green Leafhopper (Nephotettix virescens), are small but highly consequential pests in rice production. While they do feed directly on plant sap by piercing leaf tissue, their most devastating impact is as the primary vector of Rice Tungro Disease, the most destructive viral disease of rice in tropical Asia. Infected plants show characteristic yellow-orange discoloration, stunted growth, and reduced tillering. The virus is acquired rapidly by a leafhopper after feeding on an infected plant for just a few minutes, and can then be transmitted to a healthy plant almost immediately. Even low leafhopper populations can cause serious yield loss if Tungro virus is present in the area. Early-season monitoring of leafhopper activity is therefore critical for disease prevention.

• Egg (leaf tissue): Females insert eggs singly into leaf tissue, typically along the midrib; eggs hatch in 6–9 days; females can transmit Tungro virus to the plant while laying. 

• Nymph: Nymphs pass through 5 instars over 12–17 days; they are capable of acquiring and transmitting Tungro virus even in the earliest instars; nymphs feed actively on leaf sap. 

• Adult: Adults are mobile and highly efficient vectors; a single adult can transmit Tungro to a healthy plant after just minutes of feeding; adults live 15–30 days. 

• Total cycle: ~25 days.
• Encouraging natural predators like hunting spiders and tiny egg parasitoids.\n\n• Promoting healthy frog populations in the paddies.

• Synchronous planting to prevent continuous food supply across seasons.

• Crop rotation with non-host plants (like legumes) during the dry season.

• Destroying weed hosts surrounding the field.
• Applying seed treatments before planting.\n\n• Spraying recommended insecticides only if Tungro virus symptoms are detected alongside the hoppers.

Skippers (family Hesperiidae) in the context of rice pests are commonly referred to as rice leaf folders. The adult is a small, fast-flying butterfly, but it is the larval stage that causes crop damage. After hatching, the larva spins silk threads to fold or roll a single rice leaf lengthwise, creating a protective tube in which it lives and feeds by scraping the green tissue from the inner surface, leaving behind white, papery streaks. Heavy infestations produce fields with many white, rolled leaves, signaling significant loss of photosynthetic area. The pest is favored by dense planting and high nitrogen fertilizer application, which produce lush, succulent foliage. While individual larvae cause limited damage, large populations during the tillering stage can reduce the leaf area index enough to affect yield.

• Egg: Females lay single eggs on the upper or lower surface of rice leaves; eggs hatch in 4–6 days. 

• Larva (leaf-folder): Newly hatched larvae immediately spin silk threads to fold a leaf into a protective tube, feeding on the green tissue from inside; they pass through 5–6 instars over 15–20 days, creating characteristic white, papery streaks and rolled leaves. 

• Pupa: Pupation occurs inside the folded leaf or in the soil; the pupal stage lasts 7–10 days. 

• Adult Butterfly: Adults are fast-flying skippers that feed on nectar and lay eggs back on rice leaves. 

• Total cycle: ~30 days.
• Relying heavily on natural predators; skipper populations are usually kept naturally low by spiders, predatory crickets, and parasitic wasps.
• Reducing dense planting and lowering nitrogen fertilizer use to prevent overly succulent leaves.\n\n• Manual removal and crushing of the folded leaves.
• Chemical control is rarely recommended or necessary for skippers, as they rarely cause enough defoliation to impact yield.

The Golden Apple Snail (Pomacea canaliculata), locally known as kuhol, is an introduced invasive species from South America that has become one of the most destructive pests in Philippine rice paddies. It feeds voraciously on young rice seedlings and transplants at and below the waterline, often clipping them entirely at the base within days of flooding. A single snail can destroy multiple seedlings per night. The pest is easily identified by its bright pink to orange egg clusters, which are laid in masses above the waterline on stalks, canal walls, and other structures. The eggs hatch within 1–2 weeks, releasing hundreds of juvenile snails into the field. The Golden Apple Snail thrives in flooded conditions and spread rapidly through irrigation canals. Its introduction into Philippine agriculture in the 1980s has caused billions of pesos in annual crop losses.

• Egg: Females lay bright pink-to-orange egg masses (100–500 eggs per clutch) above the waterline on plant stalks, canal walls, and other structures; eggs hatch in 7–14 days and fall into the water. 

• Juvenile: Hatchlings drop into the water and immediately begin feeding on algae and then soft plant tissue; juveniles grow rapidly and reach reproductive maturity in 2–3 months. 

• Adult Snail: Adults can live for over a year, continuously laying egg masses every 1–2 weeks; they can survive dry conditions by burrowing into the soil and sealing their shells (estivation). 

• Total cycle: 60–90 days to maturity.
• Releasing ducks into the paddies during fallow periods or before transplanting so they can eat juvenile snails.

• Handpicking adult snails and actively crushing the pink egg masses on stalks.

• Constructing small, deep canals along the field edges to herd snails for easy mass collection.

• Managing water levels (keeping it shallow during seedling stages).
• Applying approved molluscicides (e.g., Niclosamide) to localized canal areas, specifically immediately after transplanting when seedlings are most vulnerable.

The Rice Black Bug (Scotinophara coarctata) is a shiny, dark-colored true bug (Hemiptera) that is a significant pest in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice in Southeast Asia, including the Philippines. Both nymphs and adults feed by inserting their stylet mouthparts into the leaf sheaths at the base of tillers to extract sap, weakening the plant. The most severe symptom of infestation is “bugburn,” characterized by yellowing and deadening of tillers at the stem base that can resemble drought stress. Feeding at the booting and heading stages can result in sterile panicles and empty grains. Rice black bugs are nocturnal, hiding at the base of plants during the day and aggregating at field margins near weedy vegetation. They are migratory, attracted to lights during the full moon, and tend to multiply rapidly in areas with reduced natural enemy populations.

• Egg: Females lay rows of 14–30 eggs arranged in a neat line on rice leaves; eggs hatch in 5–7 days and are light-colored before darkening. 

• Nymph: Nymphs pass through 5 instars over 30–45 days; early instars are light brown and aggregate in groups; later instars darken progressively toward the adult black coloration; all instars feed on sap at the base of tillers. 

• Adult: Shiny black adults are nocturnal, hiding at the base of plants during the day; they are migratory and attracted to bright lights during the full moon. 

• Total cycle: 45–60 days.
• Mass application of Metarhizium anisopliae (a green muscardine fungus) which naturally infects and kills the bugs.
• Setting up intense high-wattage light traps during the week of the full moon to catch migrating adults.\n\n• Temporarily raising paddy water levels to drown eggs and nymphs at the base.
• Spraying synthetic pyrethroids, but strictly as a last resort if populations explode during the highly vulnerable booting stage of the crop.

Slant-faced grasshoppers (Atractomorpha spp. and related species) are large, elongated orthopterans that get their name from their distinctively angled facial profile. In rice fields, they are considered occasional rather than primary pests, typically feeding along the margins of fields or in areas adjacent to grass-covered embankments (dikes). Both nymphs and adults consume rice leaves by chewing from the edges inward, leaving ragged, notched margins. Their coloration—ranging from green to brown—provides exceptional camouflage among rice foliage, making detection difficult. Damage tends to be concentrated at field borders and rarely reaches yield-threatening levels across an entire paddock unless large aggregations appear. They are most active in the early morning and late afternoon, and their egg pods are buried in the soil near field margins.

• Egg (soil pods): Females deposit egg pods containing 30–60 eggs into the soil near field margins; the eggs are protected by a frothy secretion that hardens; incubation takes 2–4 weeks depending on soil temperature. 

• Nymph: Nymphs closely resemble adults but are smaller and wingless; they pass through 5–6 instars over 30–40 days, feeding on rice leaves from the margins inward; excellent camouflage makes detection difficult. 

• Adult: Winged adults are more mobile and may migrate short distances; they continue feeding on leaves and lay egg pods in nearby soil. 

• Total cycle: 60–80 days.
• Encouraging insectivorous birds in the surrounding environment.\n\n• Utilizing naturally occurring entomopathogenic fungi.
• Sweeping nets to manually clear specific infested margins of the field.\n\n• Plowing and harrowing the soil to expose and destroy buried egg pods.
• Spot-spraying specific heavily infested borders rather than blanket-spraying the entire field, as these are rarely widespread primary pests.

Leaf beetles of the family Chrysomelidae that attack rice include the Rice Hispa (Dicladispa armigera), a small, spiny beetle with a distinctive dark blue-black color. Adult beetles damage rice by scraping the upper surface of leaves, leaving white, translucent streaks parallel to the leaf veins. The larvae are more damaging: they mine inside the leaf tissue between the upper and lower epidermis, creating irregular, whitish tunnels or blotches visible to the naked eye. Heavily infested leaves turn white and wither, resembling drought stress. The pest is more common in direct-seeded fields and during periods of water stress. Outbreaks are associated with dense stands and grassy weeds on field dikes that serve as alternate breeding hosts. While rarely causing total crop failure, severe infestations during the vegetative stage can significantly reduce photosynthetic capacity and overall yield.

• Egg: Females lay eggs individually on the leaf surface or inside leaf tissue in small clusters; eggs hatch in 4–7 days. 

• Larva (leaf miner): Newly hatched larvae immediately bore into the leaf and begin mining between the upper and lower epidermis, creating white, irregular tunnels or blotches; they pass through 3–4 instars over 10–15 days; adults also scrape the leaf surface, leaving white streaks. 

• Pupa: Pupation occurs inside the mined leaf or in the soil near the plant; the pupal stage lasts 5–8 days. 

• Adult Beetle: Dark blue-black spiny adults emerge, continue leaf scraping, and mate. 

• Total cycle: 25–35 days.
• Conserving tiny egg parasitoid wasps that specifically target beetle eggs.
• Clipping the top leaves of seedlings before transplanting (which removes laid eggs).\n\n• Slashing and managing grassy weeds around the dikes that serve as alternate hosts.
• Using systemic granular insecticides applied to the soil if severe white streaking is observed across the majority of seedlings.

Locusts (Locusta migratoria and related species) are among the most feared agricultural pests in history due to their capacity for mass migration and catastrophic crop destruction. In the Philippines, the migratory locust and the oriental migratory locust are the primary species of concern. Under favorable conditions (warm temperatures and crowding), solitary locusts transform into the gregarious phase, changing in behavior, body color, and size. These gregarious individuals form swarms that can number in the billions, traveling long distances and consuming virtually all vegetation in their path. In rice fields, both the nymph (hopper) bands and adult swarms strip leaves, stems, and panicles rapidly. Locusts are distinct from common grasshoppers in their ability to undergo this phase change. Hopper control during the nymph stage, before wings develop, is the most effective strategy for preventing a full-scale swarm.

• Egg (soil): Females lay egg pods of 30–100 eggs into the soil in dry, open areas; eggs can remain dormant for extended periods during unfavorable conditions; incubation lasts 2–4 weeks. 

• Nymph (Hopper): Wingless nymphs (called "hoppers") emerge and immediately aggregate in large bands; they pass through 5–6 instars over 30–40 days; hopper bands are the most controllable stage, before wings develop. 

• Adult: Fully winged adults are capable of long-distance flight; under crowding and warmth, solitary adults transform into the gregarious phase—changing color, behavior, and forming destructive swarms. 

• Total cycle: 50–70 days.
• Spraying biological control agents like Metarhizium acridum, a fungus highly specific to locusts and grasshoppers.
• Tilling the soil to desiccate buried egg pods.\n\n• Hand-catching or netting nymphs before they develop wings and mobility.
• Applying approved contact insecticides specifically targeting the concentrated hopper (nymph) stage before they mature and swarm.

Rice bugs, particularly Leptocorisa oratorius and Leptocorisa acuta (family Alydidae), are significant pests during the reproductive stage of rice. Though commonly grouped under the broader “coreid bug” label, they are correctly classified under Alydidae (broad-headed bugs). Both adults and nymphs are equipped with needle-like piercing-sucking mouthparts that they insert into developing rice grains from the pre-flowering to soft dough stage, extracting the liquid grain contents. Agricultural impact is severe and wide-ranging: feeding causes grains to become empty, chalky, partially formed, or discolored (known as “pecky” rice), directly reducing yield quantity and milling recovery quality. Their feeding punctures also serve as entry points for fungal and bacterial grain pathogens. Rice attacked by these bugs is reported to have an unpleasant odor even after cooking. In the Philippines, rice bug infestations have been estimated to cause 10–40% crop losses. The bugs are typically found in grassy areas at field margins during the vegetative stage, migrating into the paddy once panicles emerge and grain-filling begins. When disturbed, they emit a strong, foul-smelling defensive secretion. Population explosions are commonly linked to staggered planting schedules across a landscape, which provide a continuous supply of grain-filling crops, as well as the presence of extensive grassy weed areas near canals and field borders that serve as off-season breeding habitats.

• Egg (rows): Females lay neat double rows of 10–20 shiny, dark eggs on rice leaves, usually on the upper surface; eggs hatch in 5–8 days; newly laid eggs are green, darkening before hatching. 

• Nymph: Nymphs pass through 5 instars over 20–30 days; early instars are brightly colored and aggregate in groups; all instars are equipped with piercing mouthparts and feed on developing grain from the earliest stages; they emit a foul defensive odor when disturbed. 

• Adult: Adults are slender, green to brownish bugs; they are highly mobile, migrating from field margins into paddies as panicles emerge; adults live 20–30 days and continue feeding and mating. 

• Total cycle: 35–45 days.
• Conserving parasitic wasps (like Gryon species) that specifically lay their own eggs inside the coreid bug\'s eggs.

• Removing grassy weeds from field borders where they hide.

• Harvesting the crop at the optimal time to prevent late-stage feeding damage.

• Using attractant traps (like rotting snail meat or specific baits) to draw them away from grains.
• Spraying synthetic insecticides only if field sampling shows a high population actively piercing the developing milky grains.
